page.permissionsBody: In addition to Section 118, land in Himachal Pradesh may be subject to forest regulations, eco-sensitive zone notifications, municipal building by-laws, agricultural land-use restrictions and other central or state rules that limit what a buyer can do with the land after purchase. HimLand Check does not check compliance with any of these rules. Before completing a purchase, ask a qualified advocate and the relevant department — Revenue, Forest, Town and Country Planning or Municipal — whether any restriction, permission requirement or pending proceeding affects the plot. HimLand Check does not carry out any check under the Forest (Conservation) Act, the Environment Protection Act, the Himachal Pradesh Town and Country Planning Act or under any municipal scheme. Those checks require specialist knowledge and official records that are not publicly available online. Before purchasing any land, ask the Revenue Department whether the plot is subject to a land ceiling notification, and ask the Forest Department whether any part of the plot falls within a reserved or protected forest boundary. These checks are outside what HimLand Check can provide.

section118.title: Section 118 and who can buy land
section118.body: Section 118 of the H.P. Tenancy and Land Reforms Act, 1972 restricts the purchase of agricultural land in Himachal Pradesh by non-agriculturists. If you are not an agriculturist as defined by the Act, you need prior permission from the state government before buying agricultural land. The restriction applies regardless of whether the land is currently being farmed. HimLand Check does not assess eligibility — confirm your status and the land's classification with a qualified advocate and the Revenue Department before entering into any agreement.

Home.checklistTitle: A pre-purchase check is not optional
Home.checklistBody: Land disputes in Himachal Pradesh can remain unresolved for years. A plot may show a clear jamabandi entry and still have a pending civil suit, an unattested mutation, or a mortgage that was not released on the records. The only way to surface these issues before money changes hands is to check every relevant document and official portal in a consistent order. HimLand Check gives you the tools and the checklist; the checks themselves require you to open the official portals, complete the CAPTCHAs and retrieve certified copies. The nakal checker is a starting point, not a conclusion. Use it to identify the entries that need follow-up, then verify each one at the official source. A clean checker result means only that the uploaded document had no flags the rules detected — it does not mean the plot is free of issues that the document does not record.

limits.title: Why these checks require a person
limits.body: HimBhoomi and eCourts use CAPTCHAs to prevent automated access. HimLand Check does not bypass those controls or impersonate a user at any official source. The verification workspace standardises the information you carry into each portal, keeps your plot brief consistent, and structures your evidence trail — but every step that touches an official portal requires you to open it, complete any CAPTCHA, and retrieve the document yourself. That is by design: the official record you retrieve is the evidence; a screenshot of a third-party summary is not.

Verification.whyOwnership: The jamabandi records who holds the land and in what share, but ownership can be more complicated than a single entry. Where multiple khewats exist, or where a mutation has been recorded but not yet attested, the picture in the current nakal may not match what the seller claims. Always read every khasra entry for the plot, trace the mutation chain, and confirm that the seller's name appears as the recorded owner in the most recent attested entry.
Verification.whyMutation: A mutation (intkal) is the revenue entry made when ownership or occupancy changes — through sale, inheritance, gift, court order or partition. A mutation that is pending or rejected does not establish title. If the jamabandi shows a pending mutation, do not proceed until you have confirmed its current status at the Tehsil office and obtained an attested copy of the entry.
Verification.whyCourt: An adverse court order — a stay, an injunction or a decree — may not appear in the jamabandi at all. Revenue records and civil court records are maintained separately. Searching the eCourts portal for every person named in the jamabandi as an owner or prior owner is the only way to identify litigation that has not yet been reflected in the revenue entry.
Verification.evidenceBody: Save a copy of everything you retrieve: the jamabandi nakal with its receipt number, the HimBhoomi or BhuNaksha screenshots, and any court-portal search results. Keep the date and time of each search. If a dispute arises later, a dated record of what the official portals showed at the time of your enquiry demonstrates the due diligence you carried out. If you use the verification workspace, the brief it generates records the plot identifiers, owner names and search terms in a consistent form. Use the same brief for every portal you search. Consistency in spelling and in the khasra number format matters: HimBhoomi, HimRIS and the eCourts portal each have different search interfaces, and a name entered differently in each portal may return different results. The workspace helps you carry the same information through every check without variation.
Verification.summaryBody: Before completing a purchase: retrieve the current attested jamabandi nakal from HimBhoomi and confirm the recorded owner, khasra number and area; check that all mutations in the chain are attested and that none are pending; search the eCourts portal for every person named in the ownership column; check the BhuNaksha map and confirm the boundary and area match the nakal; look up the applicable circle rate and confirm that the agreed price meets the minimum; obtain certified copies of every document the seller provides; and confirm with an advocate that no Section 118 or other restriction applies to your transaction. Keep all retrieved documents and screenshots in a single folder with the retrieval date in the file name. A dated evidence record is your best protection if a dispute arises after the sale is complete.

Tools.howBody: Most land checks in Himachal Pradesh require more than one document. Start with the jamabandi search to retrieve the current record of rights for the village and khasra. Upload the nakal to the checker to scan for mutation entries, court-case remarks and mortgage notes that need follow-up. Open the plot map to confirm the parcel boundary matches the khasra number and the area stated in the record. Look up the circle rate for the district and Sub-Registrar office to understand the government valuation benchmark, then use the stamp duty calculator to estimate registration costs. Run the full verification checklist last, using the brief the workspace generates, before you open the official portals to confirm each item. Each tool is independent — use them in any order that suits your review.
Tools.recordsBody: The search and nakal checker work with jamabandi records from HimBhoomi. A jamabandi is Himachal Pradesh's principal record of rights: it records each khewat (estate), the khasra plots within it, the recorded owners and their shares, the land area and use, and the mutation history up to the last settlement. The map tool covers parcels indexed in BhuNaksha for the districts where parcel data is published. Circle-rate schedules are the PDFs published by the Registration and Stamps Department through the MEGH portal.

whoBenefits.title: Who benefits from these tools
whoBenefits.body: Prospective buyers use the search and nakal checker to verify ownership, trace mutations and spot remarks before making an offer. Sellers use the search to pull the current nakal and confirm that the revenue entry matches what they intend to transfer. Advocates and property consultants use the verification checklist to run a structured due-diligence review for clients. Patwaris and revenue officers can cross-check the circle-rate schedules and confirm land-area conversions when preparing records. The land converter is also useful for anyone reading an older revenue record where the area is stated in bigha or biswa and needs to be compared with a new survey in square metres.

doIneed.q: Do I need an account to use the tools?
doIneed.a: The search, map, converter, circle-rate and stamp-duty tools are available without an account. The nakal checker and the verification checklist require a sign-in. Saving a search and generating a pre-purchase report also require an account.

official.a: The search retrieves records directly from HimBhoomi and displays what that portal returns. The map opens the official BhuNaksha viewer. Circle-rate PDFs are linked from MEGH. These are copies of official data, not certified originals. For a legally valid copy, obtain a certified nakal from the Patwari or Tehsil office.

coverage.q: Which districts and tehsils are covered?
coverage.a: The search covers every district, tehsil and revenue village that HimBhoomi makes available through its public interface. BhuNaksha coverage varies by tehsil — some areas have complete parcel data and others do not. Circle-rate schedules are available for the Sub-Registrar offices whose notices the MEGH portal lists.

languages.q: Are the tools available in Hindi?
languages.a: Yes. The platform supports English and Hindi throughout. Switch language using the selector in the navigation bar. The revenue record content — owner names, village names, khasra numbers — appears as HimBhoomi returns it, which is typically in Hindi or transliterated form regardless of the interface language you have chosen. The converter labels — kanal, marla, bigha, biswa — are fixed in English in both language modes because they are technical terms that do not translate cleanly into the measurement names used in everyday Hindi conversation in every district.

CircleRateTool.title: Himachal Pradesh Circle Rates
CircleRateTool.intro: Find and download official government circle-rates in Himachal Pradesh.
CircleRateTool.lookupHelp: Select a district and SRO to see available notices. Open the PDF and check its effective period, land category and unit.

CircleRateTool.overviewBody: A circle-rate schedule gives you a starting point for valuing land for registration. Use it to compare the proposed purchase price with the notified valuation and budget for transaction costs. Start with the notice issued for the office that covers the property. If the circle rate for a category is not listed separately, check whether the schedule has a default rate that applies to all unlisted categories, or ask the Sub-Registrar.
CircleRateTool.readTitle: What to check in the notice
CircleRateTool.readLocation: Match the revenue village or locality to your land record and check when the notice applies.
CircleRateTool.readCategory: Find the row for your land use. Check whether the schedule has a separate category based on road access or distance.
CircleRateTool.readUnit: Read the rate and its unit together. Convert the plot area to that unit before estimating its value.

lookup.q: How do I download a circle-rate notice?
lookup.a: Choose your district and Sub-Registrar Office. Select Find reports, then Download PDF beside the relevant notice. Use the effective period printed in the PDF to pick the correct file.

meaning.q: Is the circle rate the sale price?
meaning.a: The circle rate is a registration valuation benchmark. The sale price is the amount the buyer and seller agree to.

variation.q: Can two plots in the same village have different rates?
variation.a: Yes. A schedule may list different rates by land category or distance from a road. Read the row and any notes that apply to your plot.

date.a: Check the effective period in the official schedule for your transaction date. The date shown in the results table is the upload date.

unit.q: What if my land record uses a different area unit?
unit.a: Convert the recorded area into the unit listed in the notice before multiplying. For example, a rate per square metre requires the area in square metres.

valuation.q: How does the circle rate help estimate stamp duty?
valuation.a: Use the notice to estimate the assessed value of the property. Then enter that value and the agreed price in the stamp duty calculator for a sale-deed estimate.

missing.q: What if the PDF does not list my village?
missing.a: Check the SRO jurisdiction and whether the village appears under another spelling or a revenue estate name. Ask the Sub-Registrar which notice and row apply if you still cannot find it.

update.q: How often are circle rates updated?
update.a: Circle rates in Himachal Pradesh are revised periodically by the state government. The effective period is printed in the official schedule PDF. Download the most recent notice for your Sub-Registrar office and verify its effective date before using it for a transaction. Rates in force at the date of registration are the ones that apply.

convert.q: How do I apply the rate to a plot in kanal?
convert.a: If the circle-rate schedule states a rate per square metre, convert the recorded area to square metres first using the Himachal converter. Multiply the converted area by the rate to get the circle-rate value. Then compare that value with the agreed sale price to determine which is higher — the higher figure is the base for stamp duty.

CircleRateTool.contextTitle: What circle rates are used for
CircleRateTool.contextBody: Circle rates in Himachal Pradesh are set by the Registration and Stamps Department and published through the MEGH portal as district- and office-specific schedules. They serve as the minimum valuation floor for registration: the stamp duty on a transfer cannot be calculated on a value lower than the applicable circle rate for the land category and location. If the agreed sale price is higher than the circle rate, stamp duty is calculated on the sale price. If the agreed price is lower, the circle rate value is used instead. Understanding the applicable circle rate before negotiating a price helps you budget accurately for registration costs and avoids surprises at the Sub-Registrar office.
CircleRateTool.categoryBody: Most circle-rate schedules in Himachal Pradesh separate land into categories — agricultural, orchard, residential, commercial — and may further subdivide by distance from a metalled road or by the revenue village or locality. A plot described as agricultural in the jamabandi may attract a different rate than the same plot after a land-use change has been approved. Read the category row that matches the current land-use entry in the official record, not what the seller describes it as. If the schedule lists a road-distance criterion, check the measurement against the actual access route.

plotNumber.question: Where do I find the Plot / Khasra No.?
plotNumber.answer: Look for the Khasra number in the Jamabandi for that revenue village. Enter it exactly as shown, including any slash or subdivision.

openReport.question: How do I view or save the plot report?
openReport.answer: Choose the district, tehsil or sub-tehsil, and village. Enter the Khasra number and click Open Map. The official report opens in a new tab. If the report loads, use your browser’s Print option to save a PDF.

missingReport.question: What if the map does not open?
missingReport.answer: Check the full location and Khasra number against your land record. If they match and the report still fails to load, try the official BhuNaksha viewer or ask the local revenue office about map availability.

ownership.question: Can I use BhuNaksha to confirm ownership?
ownership.answer: Use BhuNaksha to identify the mapped parcel. Check ownership separately against the current revenue record and the relevant registered documents.

boundary.question: How do I confirm the boundary on the ground?
boundary.answer: Compare the mapped outline with the village shajra or Tatima. For a boundary stakeout or dispute, ask the local revenue office about official demarcation.

subdivision.question: What if a khasra number has been sub-divided?
subdivision.answer: Sub-divisions are recorded as mutations in the jamabandi and are reflected in the BhuNaksha map once the digital cadastre is updated. If the revenue record shows a sub-divided khasra (for example, 128/1 and 128/2) and the map only shows the original parcel, ask the Patwari to confirm the boundary of the specific sub-plot. The jamabandi entry remains the controlling record for area and ownership.

section118map.question: Does the map show Section 118 restrictions?
section118map.answer: No. BhuNaksha shows parcel boundaries, not legal restrictions on transfer. Section 118 of the H.P. Tenancy and Land Reforms Act, 1972 restricts agricultural land transfers to non-agriculturists. That restriction must be checked separately — through the Tehsil office and with a qualified advocate — before entering into any agreement.

MapExplorer.notice: Always compare the online outline with the official shajra, field book and demarcation on the ground.
MapExplorer.contextTitle: What BhuNaksha shows and what it does not
MapExplorer.contextBody: BhuNaksha is Himachal Pradesh's online parcel mapping system. It publishes the cadastral boundaries — the mapped outlines — of khasra plots as they were drawn at the last revenue settlement. The map shows each parcel's shape, its khasra number, and its relationship to neighbouring plots and to the revenue village boundary. It does not show current ownership, pending mutations, encumbrances or court orders; those are recorded in the jamabandi and are available through HimBhoomi. BhuNaksha coverage is not uniform across the state — some tehsils have fully digitised parcel maps while others have partial or no published data. If the map does not load for a plot, the parcel may not yet be in the digital BhuNaksha layer for that village. Where parcel data is not yet published for a tehsil, the BhuNaksha viewer will return an empty result or show no parcel for the entered khasra number. In that case, ask the Patwari for a manual tatima sketch and use it alongside the revenue record to understand the plot's boundaries.

tatima.title: BhuNaksha and the Tatima
tatima.body: A tatima is the official field sketch prepared by the Patwari for a specific khasra or sub-division. It shows the plot's boundaries in relation to neighbouring parcels, roads, water channels and landmarks. A tatima is different from BhuNaksha: BhuNaksha is the digital cadastral map for the whole revenue village, while a tatima is a Patwari-certified sketch for a specific plot. If a seller provides a tatima, compare it against the BhuNaksha outline for the same khasra number. Discrepancies in shape, area or boundary points should be verified with the Patwari before you proceed.

page.intro: Himachal Pradesh is one of the most sought-after and most tightly regulated land markets in India. The rules depend on who you are, what kind of land you are buying and where it sits. This guide follows the order a careful buyer should work in: eligibility first, then the record, the cost, the registration and the steps after it.

overview.title: Why Himachal is different
body: Section 118 of the Himachal Pradesh Tenancy and Land Reforms Act, 1972 restricts the transfer of land to people who are not agriculturists in the state. It is not only an outsider rule: a Himachali who does not hold agricultural land can also need permission.

On top of that, a very large part of the state is recorded forest, many areas sit inside eco-sensitive or heritage zones, and stamp duty differs between residents and non-residents. A plot that looks cheap and clear can still be impossible to register or build on.

whoNeeds.title: Who needs Section 118 permission
whoNeeds.intro: This is a simplified view. Your exact position depends on your status and on how the land is classified, so confirm it before you sign an agreement.

items.exemptAgri: Usually no permission: a Himachal agriculturist buying agricultural land, supported by the agricultural records.
items.exemptBuilt: Usually no permission: built-up property inside a municipal corporation, municipal committee or notified area.
items.exemptHimuda: Usually no permission: property allotted by HIMUDA, which is why it is often the simplest route for outsiders.
items.exemptInherit: Usually no permission: transfer to legal heirs by inheritance or gift. Stamp duty and mutation still apply.
items.needNonAgri: Permission needed: a Himachali who is not an agriculturist and wants to buy land.
items.needOutsider: Permission needed: a non-Himachali Indian citizen buying land, including plain plots outside municipal limits.

whoNeeds.note: If permission is required and not obtained, the sale deed cannot be registered, and a transaction built to get around the rule is at serious risk of being treated as void.

permission.title: What the permission covers, and the clock that starts running
body: Permission is granted for a stated purpose and a limited area. Figures commonly quoted are up to 500 square metres for a residential house and up to 300 square metres for a shop or office, with larger limits for horticulture or other approved purposes. Treat these as a starting point and read the actual order.

Once permission is granted, the land has to be put to the stated use within the time given in the order, commonly two years with a possible extension. Land left unused beyond that can vest in the State. If you are buying a plot that already carries a permission, check the date and confirm the deadline has not passed.
permission.note: Ask the seller for the original permission order and check it against the khasra number, the area and the purpose, not just the date.

amendments.title: The December 2024 amendments
body: Proposals to let non-agriculturists buy completed flats of up to 500 square metres in RERA-registered projects without permission drew strong opposition and remain contested. Because the core law has constitutional protection, do not rely on any such exemption until a Himachal lawyer has confirmed that it is in force and applies to your purchase.

cost.title: Stamp duty and registration costs
cost.intro: Commonly reported rates are listed below. Slabs and concessions change, so confirm the current figures with the Sub-Registrar or the registration portal before you fix your budget.

items.resMale: Resident male buyer: stamp duty of about 6% for higher-value property, with lower slabs for smaller ones.
items.resFemale: Resident female buyer: about 4% up to a value threshold, and higher above it.
items.resJoint: Resident joint buyers (male and female): about 5%.
items.nonRes: Non-resident buyer: a flat 12%, regardless of gender. A second home or a temporary stay in the state does not make you a resident.
items.reg: Registration fee: 2% of the market value or the price, whichever is higher, with a minimum of ₹100 and rounded to the nearest ₹10, for a sale or gift deed.
items.estamp: Payment: e-stamping is mandatory, and physical stamp paper has been discontinued since April 2024.

cost.note: Duty is charged on the higher of the circle rate or the agreement value. On a ₹1 crore property, 12% is ₹12 lakh against ₹6 lakh at 6%, so your resident status can change the budget by lakhs.

records.title: Check the records before you pay
records.intro: Run these checks yourself on a fresh record, not on printouts supplied by the seller.

items.jamabandi: Jamabandi: confirm the seller is the recorded owner, the land is private (not government or forest) and the area matches.
items.girdawari: Khasra girdawari: confirm how the land is actually being used and that it matches what the seller says.
items.mutation: Mutation (intkal): confirm the seller’s own purchase or inheritance has been mutated in their name. A pending mutation means title has not fully moved.
items.govtBank: Government land bank: confirm the plot is not listed as government land, which cannot be sold privately.
items.circle: Circle rate: find the road-proximity category for the khasra, because it sets the value on which duty is charged.
items.encumbrance: Encumbrance: look for any mortgage, charge or earlier unresolved sale against the property.
items.residency: Your status: confirm whether you will be treated as a resident or a non-resident for stamp duty.
items.s118: Section 118: confirm which category you fall in, and whether permission is needed, already held or exempt.

process.title: The registration process, step by step

items.a: Verify the jamabandi, khasra and mutation on HimBhoomi and obtain a fresh certified nakal.
items.b: Settle Section 118: hold the permission, or get written confirmation of why an exemption applies.
items.c: Work out the circle rate category, the stamp duty and the registration fee.
items.d: Pay the stamp duty by e-stamp and keep the certificate.
items.e: Draft the sale deed with the khasra and khewat numbers, village, tehsil, district, area and the permission reference.
items.f: Enter the document on the registration portal and book an appointment with the Sub-Registrar.
items.g: Attend in person: buyer, seller and two witnesses with identity documents, including biometric verification.
items.h: After registration, apply for mutation so the revenue record shows you as the owner.

process.note: For a purchase above ₹50 lakh, the buyer may have to deduct 1% TDS and deposit it using Form 26QB. Ask your adviser how this applies to your deal.

zones.title: Special zones that can limit what you build

items.shimla: Shimla: a heritage precinct, height limits and construction orders from the courts and the NGT. Check the current development plan.
items.manali: Manali and Kullu: parts are eco-sensitive, with restrictions near the Beas river and forested slopes.
items.kasauli: Kasauli: cantonment rules apply alongside state law, so Cantonment Board clearance may be needed.
items.parks: Near national parks and sanctuaries: land inside the eco-sensitive zone, commonly up to 10 km, may need wildlife board clearance before construction.
items.tribal: Kinnaur, Spiti and Lahaul: extra restrictions can apply in some high-altitude and border areas. Ask the District Collector.
items.industrial: Baddi, Barotiwala and Nalagarh: industrial investment can have separate routes, but residential plots still need permission for non-Himachalis.

nri.title: If you are an NRI or OCI
body: For NRIs, the practical route is usually built-up property in a municipal area or a HIMUDA allotment, both of which avoid the Section 118 permission process. Payments should come through NRE or NRO accounts, and a power of attorney signed abroad has to be notarised or attested as required and then registered here.

Agricultural land and undeveloped plots are far harder: you need Section 118 permission and must also satisfy FEMA rules, which restrict NRIs from buying agricultural land. Non-resident stamp duty applies even to built-up property. Get advice before you commit.

redflags.title: Red flags: walk away or pause

items.a: A non-agriculturist buying land with no Section 118 permission.
items.b: A permission whose use deadline has passed with the land still unused.
items.c: A jamabandi that shows forest or government land.
items.d: A seller whose own mutation is not yet complete.
items.e: A plot in a heritage, eco-sensitive or cantonment area with no clearance for what you plan to build.
items.f: A builder project that is not registered with HP RERA.
items.g: A claim that an exemption applies, with no written confirmation from a lawyer.
items.h: A budget that ignores non-resident stamp duty, or a deed on physical stamp paper after April 2024.

outsider.q: Can an outsider buy land in Himachal Pradesh?
outsider.a: Not freely. A non-agriculturist, whether from outside the state or from within it, generally needs Section 118 permission to buy land. Built-up property in a municipal area and HIMUDA allotments are commonly treated differently, but confirm this for your specific property.

unpermitted.q: What happens if I buy without the required permission?
unpermitted.a: The sale deed cannot normally be registered, and a transaction structured to avoid the rule can be challenged and treated as void. Do not pay large sums before the permission position is clear.

himuda.q: Why is HIMUDA often the simplest option?
himuda.a: HIMUDA allotments are generally outside the Section 118 permission process, so buyers avoid the longest step. You still need to verify the allotment documents and pay the applicable duty.

rera.q: Do I need to check RERA?
rera.a: If you are buying into a builder project, yes. Confirm that the project is registered with HP RERA and review its approvals and progress reports before paying.

mutation.q: Why does mutation after registration matter?
mutation.a: Registration creates the sale deed, but the revenue record changes only through mutation. Without it, the jamabandi keeps showing the old owner, which causes problems later when you sell, borrow against the land or pass it on.

cta.title: Before you pay a token amount
cta.body: Pull a fresh nakal, locate the khasra on the village map, and ask a Himachal property lawyer to review the permission position and the chain of title.

legalHeir.title: Legal heir certificate in Himachal Pradesh
legalHeir.body: A legal heir certificate names the surviving heirs of a deceased owner. When land is inherited, check that every heir is listed and has agreed to the sale.
legalHeir.point1: Check that every heir, including married daughters, is listed.
legalHeir.point2: Look for written consent from each heir, with a guardian for any minor.
legalHeir.point3: Match the deceased’s name and date of death to the jamabandi.
legalHeir.metaTitle: Legal Heir Certificate in Himachal Pradesh: How to Apply and What Buyers Must Check
legalHeir.metaDescription: How a legal heir certificate works in Himachal Pradesh: who issues it, how to apply online or offline, what it contains, common defects and what land buyers should verify.

page.intro: When a landowner dies without a registered will, the land passes to the legal heirs together. A legal heir certificate is the revenue document that records who those heirs are. It matters to a buyer because a sale of inherited land is only safe if every heir is accounted for.

what.title: What the certificate is
body: It is issued by the Tehsildar or Naib Tehsildar of the Revenue Department after the Patwari checks the family details on the ground. It lists each heir with their relationship to the deceased, their age and their marital status.

It is used to update the jamabandi, to transfer inherited property, and to claim pensions, provident fund, bank balances and insurance. Where there is a valid will, the will governs, and the certificate is for cases without one.

items.issuer: Issued by: the Tehsildar or Naib Tehsildar, after Patwari verification.
items.fee: Fee: reported as a very small official fee of about ₹7, with duplicates from a Lok Mitra Kendra charged per page. Confirm the current fee on the portal.
items.time: Time: usually a day or two once the application is complete, though it can take longer if the field inquiry is slow.
items.validity: Validity: no expiry, but it reflects the family as it stood on the date of issue.
items.where: Where to apply: the HP e-District portal, or a Sugam Centre or Lok Mitra Kendra.

online.title: How to apply online

items.a: Register or log in on the HP e-District portal.
items.b: Choose the Revenue Department and then the legal heirs certificate service.
items.c: Enter the deceased’s name and date of death, then list every surviving heir: the spouse, all sons and daughters (married or not) and the parents if alive. Pay the fee online.
items.d: Track the application. After the Patwari’s inquiry and the Tehsildar’s approval, download the digitally signed certificate.

online.note: Never leave out an heir to keep things simple. An incomplete list makes the certificate defective and open to challenge later.

items.a: Collect and fill in the application form at the Tehsildar’s office or a Sugam Centre, listing all surviving family members.
items.b: Attach the death certificate, the applicant’s identity proof such as Aadhaar or voter ID, and any other document the office asks for.
items.c: Submit the form at the counter and keep the reference number.
items.d: Once the Patwari reports and the Tehsildar approves, collect the certificate. If it is lost, ask the nearest Lok Mitra Kendra for a duplicate, carrying the death certificate and your ID.

contents.title: What to read on the certificate

items.name: Deceased’s name and date of death: they should match the death certificate and the name in the jamabandi.
items.heirs: List of heirs: the spouse, children and, where applicable, parents should all appear. A missing heir is the most common source of later disputes.
items.relation: Relationship: check that each relationship is recorded correctly and that no daughter has been left out.
items.age: Age and marital status: shows whether any heir is a minor, which changes how the sale must be done.
items.authority: Issuing authority: look for the officer’s signature, the official seal and an issue date. Online copies should be digitally signed.

items.a: A married daughter is left out. Courts in Himachal have treated this as a defect, and an omitted daughter can challenge the sale.
items.b: A minor heir has no guardian. A minor cannot consent, so the sale needs a court-appointed guardian and, where the law requires it, court permission.
items.c: Only some heirs sign. A complete certificate does not help if the sale is signed by part of the family: the others keep their share and can seek partition.
items.d: A thin family inquiry. Heirs who live away or abroad can be missed, and a later claimant can contest the certificate.
items.e: The certificate is used where a court order is needed. It is a revenue document, not a court order. Lenders, high-value transfers and disputed estates may require a succession certificate from a civil court.
items.f: An out-of-date certificate. If a listed heir has since died, that heir’s own heirs now have a share, and the old certificate no longer shows the full picture.

buyers.title: Why it matters when you buy
body: For inherited land, no single heir can sell the whole plot alone. The certificate shows who the owners are, and every one of them has to agree before the sale is safe. A buyer who registers a deed signed by fewer than all heirs risks a partition or cancellation suit, sometimes years later.

Banks look for the same three things: the certificate, consent from every heir, and proof that no minor is involved without a guardian. A file missing any of them usually stalls at the lender’s legal check.
buyers.note: Red flag: a certificate that lists only sons, a seller who cannot produce written consent from the listed heirs, or one who discourages you from speaking to the rest of the family.

when.q: When is a legal heir certificate needed?
when.a: When land or other assets pass from a person who died without a registered will: for mutation, for selling inherited land, and for pension, bank and insurance claims.

docs.q: What documents are needed to apply?
docs.a: The death certificate, identity proof of the applicant and a complete list of the surviving family members.

daughter.q: Can a married daughter be left out?
daughter.a: She should not be. Daughters are generally entitled heirs, and Himachal courts have treated their omission as a defect. A certificate that leaves out a living daughter is open to challenge.

succession.q: Legal heir certificate or succession certificate?
succession.a: The legal heir certificate comes from the Tehsildar and suits routine mutation and transfers. A succession certificate comes from a civil court and may be needed for disputed estates, high-value transfers or where a lender or the Sub-Registrar asks for stronger proof.

mandatory.q: Do I need one to sell inherited land?
mandatory.a: In practice, yes. A Sub-Registrar will usually ask for proof of who the heirs are, and all of them must consent. Without these, the deed may be refused or later challenged.

validity.a: No, but it only reflects the family on the date of issue. If a listed heir has died since, a fresh or supplementary certificate may be needed.

cta.title: Before you sign for inherited land
cta.body: Ask for the certificate, written consent from every heir and the death certificate of any heir who has died. Compare the names with a fresh jamabandi and have a lawyer review the chain.

forestLand.title: How to check for forest land in Himachal Pradesh
forestLand.body: About two-thirds of Himachal is recorded forest. Read the land type in the jamabandi, then confirm with the Forest Department before you rely on a seller’s word.
forestLand.point1: Read the land type in a fresh jamabandi.
forestLand.point2: Get written confirmation from the Range Forest Officer.
forestLand.point3: Check the distance from national parks and sanctuaries.
forestLand.metaTitle: Forest Land Check in Himachal Pradesh: How to Verify Before You Buy
forestLand.metaDescription: How to check whether a plot in Himachal Pradesh is forest land: jamabandi land type, Forest Department confirmation, eco-sensitive zones, common seller tricks and red flags.

page.intro: A forest land check tells you whether a plot is recorded forest, protected forest, or close enough to a protected area to face restrictions. In Himachal, where roughly 68% of the geographic area is recorded forest, this is one of the most important checks a buyer can make, because land you cannot lawfully own or build on has little value.

what.title: What the check covers
body: Forest status is decided under the Indian Forest Act, 1927, the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 and the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972. The Revenue Department’s jamabandi shows the land type, while the Forest Department holds the forest and protected-area records.
Recorded forest is a legal classification. A plot can be recorded forest even if it has no dense tree cover, and it is the legal record that counts, not how the land looks.
what.note: A khasra recorded as Van or any forest type in the current jamabandi cannot be privately bought or built on.

online.title: How to check online

items.a: On HimBhoomi, open the land records, choose the district, tehsil and village, enter the khasra number and read the land type. If it shows Van or any forest class, stop.
items.b: On the Forest Department website, look at the notified areas and any forest clearance or diversion records for the village or khasra.
items.c: Compare the district and village against the list of national parks, sanctuaries and eco-sensitive zones.
items.d: Save the jamabandi and any references to take to your lawyer.

online.note: A plot outside a town planning area may not appear in planning records but can still overlap recorded forest. Run both checks separately.

offline.title: How to check at the forest office

items.a: Find the Range Forest Officer for the tehsil. The department has offices across all districts.
items.b: Submit the khasra number, village, tehsil and a copy of the jamabandi, and ask in writing whether the plot is recorded forest, protected forest or inside an eco-sensitive zone.
items.c: Allow the Divisional or Range Forest Officer to check the forest maps and notified boundaries.
items.d: Collect the confirmation in writing on official letterhead. A verbal assurance has no legal value.

offline.note: Near a district boundary, ask both neighbouring divisions, because forest boundaries do not always follow tehsil lines.

items.khasra: Khasra number: it must match the plot you are buying exactly.
items.landType: Land type in the jamabandi: it should be private, agricultural or non-agricultural. Van or any forest class means do not proceed without proper legal verification.
items.recorded: Recorded forest status: confirm with the Range Forest Officer whether the parcel sits inside a notified forest boundary.
items.protected: Protected-area distance: check whether the plot lies within the eco-sensitive zone of a national park or sanctuary.
items.diversion: Diversion status: if forest land was diverted for non-forest use, confirm the approval and its conditions.
items.authority: Issuing officer and date: the confirmation should rely on current records and be signed and sealed by the competent authority.

items.a: The jamabandi shows Van but the seller says it is private, pointing to old records. The current jamabandi governs, so pull it yourself from HimBhoomi.
items.b: The plot partly overlaps forest. On steep terrain one khasra can straddle private and forest land. Ask the Range Forest Officer for a boundary overlay before agreeing on area or price.
items.c: The eco-sensitive zone is not mentioned. Plots near national parks and sanctuaries can need wildlife board clearance before construction. Check the coordinates against the notified boundaries.
items.d: Forest land is sold as agricultural. Revenue and forest records sometimes disagree, especially in older villages. Run both checks together.
items.e: A clearance is described as in process. A pending diversion application is not an approval, and building before clearance can be an offence. Ask for the application number and track it on the PARIVESH portal.
items.f: Forest rights claims. Unresolved claims under the Forest Rights Act, 2006 can block development even after purchase. Ask the Divisional Forest Officer whether any are pending on the parcel.

why.title: Why this check matters
body: Land recorded as forest cannot be the subject of a valid private sale. A deed registered on it is void, and any non-forest use or construction needs central clearance.

Even private land near a protected area can face permanent limits on construction. Banks also check forest classification and eco-sensitive proximity, and a plot with any forest class will fail technical sanction.
why.note: Red flag: a seller who discourages you from visiting the forest office, says the jamabandi will be corrected after registration, or offers hillside land near forest at a price far below market.

what.q: What is a forest land check?
what.a: It is a verification that a plot is not recorded forest, protected forest or inside a restricted zone. It combines the land type in the jamabandi with confirmation from the Forest Department.

online.a: Look up the khasra on HimBhoomi and read the land type. Any forest entry means the land is off limits for private purchase. Then get written confirmation from the Range Forest Officer.

buy.a: No. Recorded, protected or reserved forest cannot be validly sold privately, and a deed on such land is void. Non-forest use also needs central clearance.

mistake.q: What if I buy forest land by mistake?
mistake.a: The sale is void under forest law, the authorities can take back the land, and structures on it can face demolition. Recourse is very limited once the deed is registered, so check first.

near.q: Does living near a national park affect me?
near.a: Yes. Plots inside the eco-sensitive zone, commonly up to 10 km from the boundary, may need wildlife board clearance before building. The exact extent is notified for each area, so check it for the park concerned.

cover.q: What is the difference between recorded forest and forest cover?
cover.a: Recorded forest is the legal classification, whether or not trees grow there. Forest cover is land that actually has tree canopy. For a purchase, the legal record is what matters.

proof.q: What proves that land is not forest?
proof.a: A current jamabandi showing a non-forest land type, plus written confirmation from the Range Forest Officer that the parcel is outside recorded forest and eco-sensitive boundaries.

cta.title: Before you commit
cta.body: Pull the latest jamabandi yourself, get written confirmation from the forest office, and keep both on file for your lawyer’s review.

article.title: 7 documents you must check before buying land in Himachal Pradesh
article.summary: Jamabandi, tatima, intkal, title deed, mortgage status, land use and Section 118 permission—what each document proves, what it does not prove and how to check it online.

sevenDocuments.title: 7 documents you must check before buying land in Himachal Pradesh
sevenDocuments.intro: Do not treat one jamabandi or one sale deed as a complete title check. These seven records answer different questions about ownership, boundaries, transfers, charges, permitted use and the buyer's eligibility.
sevenDocuments.warning: Online records are useful for preliminary checking, but they may be delayed, incomplete or informational. Before paying token money or signing an agreement, obtain current certified copies and have a Himachal property lawyer examine the complete chain.

jamabandi.title: Jamabandi (record of rights)
jamabandi.shows: The revenue record normally identifies recorded owners, their shares, cultivators or possession entries, khata and khatauni references, khasra numbers, area, land classification and remarks for the selected settlement year.
jamabandi.flags: The seller is missing, the seller owns only a share, the area or khasra differs from the offer, an old jamabandi is shown, or the remarks refer to a mortgage, stay, acquisition or disputed mutation.
jamabandi.online: On HimBhoomi, select district, tehsil, village and jamabandi year, complete the CAPTCHA and retain the receipt number. Compare the online copy with a fresh certified nakal from the competent revenue office.

tatima.title: Tatima / plot map
tatima.shows: A tatima or plot extract locates the khasra and its relationship to neighbouring plots, access and subdivisions. It helps test whether the land shown on the ground is the land described in the records.
tatima.flags: No legal access, overlap with a neighbour, an unrecorded subdivision, shape or area inconsistent with the deed, or construction outside the offered khasra.
tatima.online: Use Bhunaksha HP where mapping has been digitised. Search the correct district, tehsil, village and plot number. The Revenue Department says map availability depends on completed digitisation, so obtain an official tatima or demarcation when the online map is absent or unclear.

intkal.title: Intkal / mutation orders
intkal.shows: Mutation entries record changes proposed or attested after sale, inheritance, gift, partition, mortgage, release or a court order. The order and status explain how the current revenue entry arose.
intkal.flags: A pending, rejected or missing mutation; transfer after the seller's deed but before the current jamabandi; inconsistent buyer or area; or a mortgage entry without a later release.
intkal.online: Read every mutation number referenced in the jamabandi and ask the Patwari or Tehsil office for the mutation order and status. HimBhoomi provides the revenue copy, but do not assume a name in the latest jamabandi proves the underlying deed or mutation order is valid.

titleDeed.title: Registered title deed and chain deeds
titleDeed.shows: The registered sale, gift, exchange, partition, release or inheritance documents establish the claimed transaction and its terms. The chain should connect the present seller to earlier owners without unexplained gaps.
titleDeed.flags: Missing original or certified copy, inconsistent khasra or area, unregistered agreement presented as ownership, power-of-attorney sale concerns, absent links in the chain, or consideration and possession clauses that conflict with the facts.
titleDeed.online: Use Himachal's NGDRS registration portal for available registration services and verify document particulars with the concerned Sub-Registrar. Obtain certified copies for every material link; online deed templates are not proof that a particular deed was registered.

mortgage.title: Mortgage and encumbrance status
mortgage.shows: A proper search checks whether the property or owner is affected by a registered mortgage, charge, attachment, lease, agreement, court restraint or other encumbrance during the relevant period.
mortgage.flags: Mortgage mutation without release, bank possession or original deeds held by a lender, recent loan closure without registered satisfaction, attachment or litigation, or a search period too short to cover the title chain.
mortgage.online: Check available registered documents through NGDRS and obtain an official search or encumbrance result from the Sub-Registrar where required. Also inspect mutation remarks and obtain the lender's no-dues and release documents; one database may not reveal every equitable mortgage or court restraint.

landUse.title: Land use and development permission
landUse.shows: Revenue classification and planning permissions indicate whether the plot is agricultural, orchard, residential, commercial, forest-related or subject to planning and construction controls.
landUse.flags: Use advertised by the seller differs from the revenue classification, construction lacks permission, conversion or change-of-use approval is absent, road/access requirements are unmet, or protected/forest restrictions may apply.
landUse.online: Start with the land classification in the jamabandi and the official Revenue Department links. For development or change of land use, verify the current approval with the competent Town and Country Planning, local body and revenue authorities for that location.

section118.title: Section 118 eligibility or permission
section118.shows: Section 118 of the H.P. Tenancy and Land Reforms Act regulates transfers of land to non-agriculturists, subject to statutory exceptions and permissions. A permission letter must match the buyer, seller, land, purpose and conditions of the proposed transfer.
section118.flags: Buyer eligibility is assumed without evidence, permission is expired or for another parcel/purpose, conditions or utilisation deadlines were breached, or payment is demanded before permission and registration requirements are satisfied.
section118.online: Read the current Act, rules and Revenue Department Section 118 instructions. Verify the permission directly with the issuing authority and obtain legal advice on the buyer's status and the exact transaction; a website checklist cannot decide eligibility.

final.title: The seven documents must agree
final.body: Names, shares, khasra numbers, area, boundaries, transaction dates, mortgage releases, land use and permission conditions should form one consistent chain. Any mismatch should pause the transaction until it is resolved in writing from the competent authority.

a.q: Why must I choose the village from the official directory?
a.a: HimBhoomi uses the official district, tehsil and village codes. Selecting a listed village helps match your request to the correct revenue records.

b.q: What if I do not know the khasra number?
b.a: You can continue with the available record-number choices. If you know it, enter the khasra exactly as printed, including a slash such as 123/4.

c.q: Why does the Jamabandi year list change by village?
c.a: Years are supplied by HimBhoomi for the selected village, so older or newer records may differ between villages.

Search.howBody: The search connects to HimBhoomi — Himachal Pradesh's official land records portal — through the public interface. When you choose a district, tehsil, village and jamabandi year, the selectors load the options that HimBhoomi makes available for that combination. After you complete the CAPTCHA, HimBhoomi returns the record choices available for the selected location: Jamabandi (by khewat, khatauni or khasra number) or Shajra Nasab. Choose the identifier that matches the number in your record and load the official nakal. The receipt number returned by HimBhoomi is your reference for that specific record retrieval.
Search.whatTitle: What to look for in the record
Search.whatBody: Once the jamabandi loads, check four things. First, confirm the owner entries: the name, share and basis of ownership for every khata. Second, trace the mutation chain: each intkal entry records a change — sale, inheritance, gift, court order — with a date and status. A pending or rejected mutation needs follow-up at the Tehsil. Third, check the khasra area and land-use classification against what the seller stated. Fourth, read the remarks column: entries about mortgages, court stays or other charges appear there and are easy to miss when reading quickly. Use the nakal checker to scan these fields automatically and flag items that need attention.
Search.captchaNote: The CAPTCHA is controlled by HimBhoomi and cannot be bypassed or automated. If the CAPTCHA image does not load or the code is not accepted, use the New code button to request a fresh one. If HimBhoomi is temporarily unavailable, the search will show an error — this is a condition of the official portal and is outside our control.

About.title: About HimLand Check
About.intro: HimLand Check is a simpler way to read, understand and check government land records — for villages in Himachal Pradesh. We bring together the records held by HimBhoomi, BhuNaksha and the official Sub-Registrar notices and present them in a form that is easier to navigate before a property transaction.

whatWeDo.title: What we do
whatWeDo.body: We make public revenue records — jamabandi, khasra, khatauni, khewat, mutations — searchable in one place, show them on maps and shajra drawings, and produce pre-purchase check reports. The search covers every district, tehsil and revenue village served by the HimBhoomi portal. The map tool links each khasra number to the corresponding parcel on the BhuNaksha viewer. The nakal checker reads an uploaded jamabandi PDF and flags items — pending mutations, case references, mortgage remarks — that you would otherwise have to find by reading the document line by line. There is also a marketplace where people list land themselves; those listings are separate from the revenue data.

whatWeAreNot.title: What we are not
whatWeAreNot.body: HimLand Check is an independent private platform. It is not affiliated with or authorised by the Government of Himachal Pradesh, the Revenue Department, the Registration and Stamps Department or any other government agency. The records shown here are compiled from public sources and are for reference only. They are not a substitute for a certified government copy (nakal). A nakal issued by the competent Revenue authority — the Patwari, Tehsildar or their office — is the only document that carries legal weight in a court or transaction. Always confirm current ownership, mutation status and encumbrances with the relevant Tehsil or Patwari office before entering into any agreement.

whoRuns.title: Who runs it
whoRuns.body: Operated by {company} LLP, a limited liability partnership registered in India. The platform is built and maintained by a small team focused on making land due-diligence accessible before purchase decisions.

howItWorks.title: How it works
howItWorks.body: Records are sourced from HimBhoomi, the official Himachal Pradesh land records portal, through the public interface. The nakal checker uses an AI model — Google Gemini — to extract structured fields from the uploaded PDF, then applies a fixed set of rules to flag items for review. Circle-rate schedules are fetched directly from the MEGH document management portal and linked by district and Sub-Registrar office. BhuNaksha map reports are opened on the official government viewer; we do not store or copy map data. No data is sold and no advertising is shown.

whenToUse.title: When to use HimLand Check
whenToUse.body: HimLand Check is most useful in the period between first showing interest in a plot and signing a sale agreement. Use the search to pull the current jamabandi for the village and khasra. Use the nakal checker to scan for mutations, case remarks and mortgage entries. Use the map to confirm that the plot's shape and location match what the seller showed you. Use the circle-rate tool to check the government valuation benchmark and estimate stamp duty. Use the verification checklist to record and preserve your checks in a consistent order. At every step, confirm what you find with the Patwari or Tehsil office and obtain certified copies before any money changes hands.

contact.title: Questions and corrections
contact.body: If you have a question about how the platform works, want to report an error in the data shown, or have a request about personal information that appears in a land record, use the contact page or write to us at the address shown there. We will acknowledge the message and reply within a reasonable time.

recordTypes.title: Records the platform covers
recordTypes.body: The search and nakal checker work with jamabandi records from HimBhoomi. The jamabandi is Himachal Pradesh's principal record of rights: it records each khewat, the khasra plots within it, the recorded owners and their shares, the land area and use, the soil type, and the mutation history to the last settlement. A khewat number identifies the estate; a khatauni number identifies the occupancy record; a khasra number identifies the individual plot. The shajra-nasab is the genealogical pedigree associated with an ownership entry. The map tool covers parcels indexed in BhuNaksha. Circle-rate and stamp-duty tools use schedules from the Registration and Stamps Department published through MEGH.

limitations.title: Known limitations
limitations.body: Coverage depends on what HimBhoomi and BhuNaksha make publicly available. Older settlements and remote tehsils may have incomplete digital records. The nakal checker works best on clearly scanned PDFs from HimBhoomi; handwritten remarks or low-resolution scans reduce extraction quality. Circle-rate schedules on MEGH are updated when the state government revises rates, but the upload date in the portal may lag the gazette notification date — always check the effective period printed in the PDF. HimLand Check has no access to unpublished or confidential records. If a record is unavailable here, go to the Tehsil or Patwari office in person. Request a physical inspection copy from the Patwari for any plot where the digital record is incomplete.

If a village has been renamed or re-mapped in HimBhoomi, an older saved search may no longer return results — in that case, run a new search with the updated village name.
Dashboard.reportNote: A pre-purchase check report is generated from a jamabandi record retrieved through the search. It summarises the ownership entries, mutation history, khasra area and remarks in a structured PDF and flags items that need further verification. The report is an informational summary — it is not a title opinion, a legal search or a certified nakal. Use it as a checklist alongside the original official documents, not as a substitute for them. Reports are stored against your account and can be downloaded again from this page.
Dashboard.listingNote: If you have listed land on the marketplace, the listings panel shows the current status — active, withdrawn or sold — and lets you edit, withdraw or delete the listing. A listing is visible to other users until you withdraw it or mark it as sold. We do not verify the accuracy of listing information and are not a party to any transaction that may arise. If a listing you posted contains an error, update or delete it promptly.
Dashboard.privacyNote: Saved searches, reports and listing data are stored against your account and are not visible to other users. When you delete a saved search or report, it is removed from your dashboard. If you close your account, all data associated with it is deleted within a reasonable period as described in our Privacy Policy. Listings that have already been viewed by other users may remain briefly in search results during the deletion period.

gettingStarted.title: Getting started
gettingStarted.body: To use the dashboard, sign in with your account. If you do not have an account, register on the login page — registration requires a name, email address and phone number. Once signed in, the dashboard loads your saved searches, reports and listings automatically. The first time you sign in, all three panels will be empty. Start by running a search, uploading a nakal to the checker, or posting a land listing to populate your dashboard. If the dashboard shows an error, refresh the page. If the error persists, the database connection may be temporarily unavailable — try again after a few minutes. You can sign in with an email and password or through a supported OAuth provider if one is configured. If you have forgotten your password, use the Reset password link on the login page — a reset link will be sent to the email address registered to your account. Account registration is free. Some features — the nakal checker, report generation and saved searches — are only available to signed-in users. The nakal checker and report generator may take up to a minute to process a document — the page will show a progress indicator while the AI model reads the PDF. Do not close the tab while processing is in progress. If a timeout occurs, return to the dashboard and check whether the report was saved before the timeout. If it was not, run the check again from the search results page.

Converter.title: Land unit converter
Converter.intro: Convert Himachal land measurements without assuming one district-wide standard.
Converter.enterValue: Enter an area to see the conversion.
Converter.note: For guidance only. Measurement practice can differ by locality. Confirm the unit and area in official revenue records before relying on a conversion. For high-value transactions, have the Patwari verify the measurement on site.
Converter.standardsIntro: These reference values are not automatic district rules. Select the unit stated in your record and verify it with the Patwari or Revenue Department.
Converter.kanalStandards: 1 kanal = 20 marla; 1 marla = 19.19754225 sq m; therefore 1 kanal = 383.950845 sq m. 1 karam = 57.5 inches = 1.4605 m; 1 sq karam (sarshai) = 2.13306025 sq m; 1 ghumao = 3071.60676 sq m.
Converter.bighaStandards: 1 karam (56 inches) = 1.4224 m; 1 sq karam (biswansi) = 2.02322176 sq m; 1 biswa = 40.4644352 sq m = 20 biswansi; 1 bigha = 809.288704 sq m = 20 biswa.
Converter.exampleBody: If a record states 2 kanal, convert it to 767.90169 sq m. If it states 3 biswa, the result is 121.3933056 sq m. These examples show arithmetic only; they do not decide which standard applies. A common situation is a plot recorded as 1 kanal 5 marla. To convert: 1 kanal = 20 marla, so the total is 25 marla. 25 × 19.19754225 sq m = 479.938556 sq m. Confirm the unit with the Patwari before using this in any agreement. If the record uses the bigha system, work from the karam value stated in that settlement — do not mix the two standards.

districts.q: Does the converter choose a standard by district?
districts.a: No. Local practice and records can differ, so the converter leaves the choice to you.

which.a: Use the unit printed in the jamabandi, tatima, sale deed or other official record.

records.a: A calculator only applies supplied numbers. Confirm the unit and area with the Patwari, Tehsil or Revenue Department.

rounding.a: Documents may round karam or biswansi values. Use the official record as the controlling value.

ownership.q: Can I use the result for a registered deed?
ownership.a: No. The converter gives an arithmetic estimate. Confirm the recorded area and applicable unit directly in the official land record and with the Patwari before using any figure in a deed or agreement.

biswa.q: What is the difference between a biswa and a biswansi?
biswa.a: A biswansi is one twentieth of a biswa. Under the bigha/biswa standard used in parts of Himachal Pradesh, 1 biswa equals 20 biswansi and 1 bigha equals 20 biswa. The karam length under this standard is 56 inches, giving 1 biswansi = 2.02322176 sq m.

kanal.q: What is a kanal in Himachal Pradesh?
kanal.a: A kanal equals 20 marla. Under the standard used in most of Himachal Pradesh, 1 marla equals 19.19754225 sq m, so 1 kanal equals 383.950845 sq m. The karam under this standard is 57.5 inches. Some tehsils use slightly different values — always read the unit stated in your official record and confirm with the local Patwari.

section118.q: Does area conversion affect Section 118 eligibility?
section118.a: Section 118 of the H.P. Tenancy and Land Reforms Act, 1972 restricts the transfer of agricultural land to non-agriculturists. Eligibility depends on the nature of the transaction and the category of buyer, not on the area unit used. The converter has no bearing on Section 118 — confirm eligibility with a qualified advocate before entering into any agreement.

Converter.contextTitle: Why area units matter in Himachal land records
Converter.contextBody: Himachal Pradesh uses two parallel measurement systems inherited from pre-settlement surveys. The kanal-marla system is common in the northern and western districts and in areas that follow the Patwari karam of 57.5 inches. The bigha-biswa system is used in parts of the Shimla and Sirmour divisions and is based on a karam of 56 inches. The same plot can be described in different units depending on which settlement survey it was last entered under. When you read a jamabandi, the recorded area appears alongside the khasra number in the unit the Patwari used at settlement. The converter lets you translate that figure into square metres or square feet for comparison, but the official figure in the revenue record is always the controlling value. When a plot is sub-divided and both the original and the sub-division appear in the revenue record, check that the areas of the sub-divisions add up to the recorded area of the parent khasra. Discrepancies may indicate an unattested mutation or an error in the settlement record — flag them for confirmation with the Patwari before relying on the area in any agreement or deed.

guide.title: How the Jamabandi Checker works
guide.body: Upload a Himachal Pradesh Jamabandi PDF to review the recorded owners and shares, mutation entries, case references and possible charges that the checker can read. Compare highlighted findings with the original record and verify current details with the relevant offices.

file.a: Use a HimBhoomi Jamabandi PDF up to 4 MB. Include all pages so the checker can read remarks that continue onto later pages.

score.q: How should I read the score?
score.a: The score summarizes the checks applied to the extracted data. If fields are missing or unclear, compare them with the original PDF before drawing conclusions.

mortgage.q: What if the checker flags a mortgage?
mortgage.a: Compare the warning with the remarks in the original record. Confirm the current status with the relevant office and lender, including any release recorded since the Jamabandi was issued.

cases.q: Does the checker search for court cases?
cases.a: It reports case references it can read in the uploaded record. Check the appropriate court records separately for current case status.

privacy.a: Google Gemini processes the PDF. When the NVIDIA fallback is needed, NVIDIA receives page images. The app may reuse a result from its temporary server cache for up to six hours.

guide.contextTitle: What the checker reads and what it cannot
guide.contextBody: The checker extracts text from the uploaded PDF and applies a fixed set of rules: it looks for owner entries and shares, mutation status codes, case-reference patterns and remarks that match known mortgage or charge formats. It does not search external databases — it reads only what is in the document you uploaded. If the PDF was scanned at low resolution, or if the Patwari's handwriting in the remarks column was not captured clearly, the extraction may miss entries that are present on the paper copy. Always compare the checker's output with the original PDF before drawing any conclusions.

NakalCheck.title: Check a land record (jamabandi)
NakalCheck.intro: Upload a Jamabandi nakal PDF. We read it, run rule-based checks and show a score with the reasons. An AI model does the reading, so always compare the result with the original record.
NakalCheck.analyzing: Reading the record… this can take up to a minute.
NakalCheck.privacy: Google Gemini reads your PDF. If fallback processing is enabled and needed, NVIDIA receives images of its pages. On Google's free tier, inputs may be used to improve its models. Upload only records you are comfortable sharing with these providers.

flags.SHARE_MISMATCH: The owner shares add up to {sum}, but the record states a total of {total}. Either the record is inconsistent or it was read incorrectly.
flags.PENDING_CASE: Case {caseNo} ({caseType}) is pending in {court}, filed {filedOn}. Ownership shares or boundaries may change once the court decides.
flags.SALE_AFTER_CASE: Mutation {number} ({date}) is a transfer made after the court case was filed. Such transfers can be challenged.
flags.MANY_COOWNERS: {count} share holders own this land jointly. A seller can usually sell only a share, not a specific plot, unless the land has been partitioned.
flags.COOWNERS: {count} share holders own this land jointly. Check that every holder agrees to the sale.
flags.RAPID_TRANSFERS: {count} sales or gifts were recorded in the last {months} months. Check for plot-splitting or speculation.
flags.MUTATION_EXCEEDS_AREA: Mutation {number} transfers more area than the record shows for this land.
flags.MORTGAGE_OR_CHARGE: {count, plural, one {A mortgage or bank charge was} other {# mortgage or bank charges were}} recorded. Obtain a current release or no-dues certificate before relying on clear title.
flags.AGRI_LAND: This looks like agricultural land. In Himachal Pradesh, buying it as a non-agriculturist generally needs permission under Section 118 of the HP Tenancy and Land Reforms Act.
flags.LOW_CONFIDENCE: The reader was unsure about {count} fields. Compare the details below with the original.
flags.EXTRACTION_INCOMPLETE: Owners or the total share could not be read, so this score is not reliable.
